knowledge_type_note: Names a structural fact. Whether it is a weakness is a judgement, and the sources disagree sharply enough that the disagreement is part of the record.

attributions.note: Britannica lists doubled pawns among the structural weaknesses named by Steinitz's theory. ATTRIBUTION NOT VERIFIED: this is the conventional ascription, taken from a secondary source, and no primary text was consulted for it during this research.
The hypermodern challenge to treating them as an objective weakness.

history.notes: A widely repeated Capablanca line — 'I would take doubled pawns if in return I may place my rook on the seventh rank' — is attached to this concept in one source, which itself prefaces it 'Legend has it'. It is NOT verified and must not be quoted as Capablanca's. Recorded here only so a later session does not rediscover it and assume it is sound.
competing_claims: Classical school: doubled pawns are an objective weakness to be avoided.
Hypermodern school: dynamic compensation routinely outweighs the structural defect.

development.change: Treated as a defect to avoid.
Challenged; compensation in activity and files given equal standing.
Engines accept severe pawn defects for activity, which has moved practice towards the hypermodern view without settling it.

engine_era_note: The classical assessment is the one engines have most clearly softened. Modern practice takes doubled pawns readily for the bishop pair or an open file. The one drawback engines still price heavily is the crippled majority — doubled pawns in a majority usually cannot make a passer, and that is an endgame fact rather than an opinion.

preconditions: Two or more friendly pawns occupy the same file
indicators_for: They are also isolated, so no pawn can ever defend them
They stand on a half-open file the opponent's rooks can use
They are in a majority, which therefore cannot produce a passer unaided
The square in front of the front pawn can be blockaded by an enemy piece
The position is simplifying towards an endgame
indicators_against: The doubling opened a file that is actually being used
The bishop pair was obtained in the exchange
They increase control of central squares
They create an outpost the opponent cannot contest
They shield the king rather than exposing it
false_positive_traps: REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: doubled pawns are not automatically weak. Detecting them is trivial; concluding weakness from the detection is wrong often enough to be a real hazard.
The compensation is usually invisible to a structure check — the bishop pair and the opened file are elsewhere on the board.
Doubled CENTRAL pawns are frequently an asset, controlling four squares between them.

typical_plans: Against them: blockade the front pawn, double rooks on the file, and simplify
With them: use the opened file, play on the squares they control, and avoid endgames if the majority is crippled
Undouble by advancing and exchanging the front pawn when possible
typical_moves: bxc3 in the Nimzo-Indian, accepting the structure for the bishop pair
typical_pawn_structures: Doubled isolated pawns — the worst case
Rossolimo and Exchange Ruy structures where doubled pawns are inflicted deliberately
typical_piece_arrangements: Enemy knight blockading in front of the front pawn
strategic_consequences: A majority containing doubled pawns generally cannot make a passer unaided
The half-open file created is often the compensation

exceptions: Doubled central pawns frequently increase control and are an asset.
The exchange that doubles them often yields the bishop pair or a usable file, which is the whole point.
The recapture-towards-the-centre guideline has three standard exceptions: king shelter, a more useful file, and creating a chronic target.
limitations: Recognition is trivial; evaluation is not, and the compensating factors are usually not in the pawn structure at all.
misconceptions: That doubled pawns are a weakness. They are a concession with a price attached, and the price is often worth paying.
That the Capablanca quotation about doubled pawns and the seventh rank is verified. It is not.
That they matter equally in middlegame and endgame. They mainly bite in the endgame.
That doubled pawns are a weakness. Measured here: inflicting them cost the inflicting side 0.34, and the side that accepted them is exactly equal.

by_level.beginner: Two of your pawns are on the same file. They cannot protect each other, but the trade that put them there often gave you something in return.
by_level.intermediate: Doubled pawns on the {file}-file. Ask what the exchange bought — a file, the bishop pair, central control — before calling them a weakness.
by_level.advanced: Structural concession. The concrete drawback is the crippled majority; the compensation is usually the half-open file or the bishop pair. They bite mainly in the endgame.
by_level.master: Price them by the majority. Doubled pawns in a majority that can no longer produce a passer is a real, permanent, endgame-deciding defect; doubled central pawns with an open file beside them frequently are not.

by_depth.short: Two pawns on the {file}-file — they cannot defend each other.
by_depth.normal: Doubled pawns: two friendly pawns on one file. They cannot defend each other and the rear one is blocked, but the capture that created them usually bought something — a file, the bishop pair, or central control.
by_depth.deep: Two pawns on the same file, normally after a capture. Three real drawbacks: they cannot defend each other, the rear one is blocked, and a majority containing them usually cannot manufacture a passed pawn — which is the one engines still price heavily, because it decides endgames. Against that sit the standard compensations of an opened file, the bishop pair, extra central control and new outposts. This is a genuine disagreement between schools rather than an unsettled definition: the classical view treated them as an objective defect, the hypermoderns held that dynamics outweigh structure, and modern practice has moved towards the second without settling it.

explanations.lesson: Doubled pawns are a price, not a verdict. Ask what was bought with them — and check whether the majority they sit in can still make a passer.

definition_short: Two friendly pawns on the same file, usually after a capture. A structural concession that is frequently worth its price.
definition_long:
Two pawns of one colour on the same file. They cannot defend each other, because pawns defend diagonally; the rear pawn is blocked by the front one; and a majority containing doubled pawns usually cannot produce a passed pawn without help, which is the most concrete of the drawbacks and the one that decides endgames.

But the capture that doubles them almost always pays for something. The standard compensations: an opened or half-opened file for a rook, the bishop pair, extra control of central squares (doubled c-pawns on c3 and c4 both bear on d4 and d5), and the outposts that the new structure creates. The Nimzo-Indian 4...Bxc3+ 5.bxc3 is the classic bargain — White takes the doubled c-pawns and gets the bishop pair, a half-open b-file and a broader centre.

THIS IS A GENUINE SCHOOL DISAGREEMENT, not vagueness. The classical school (Steinitz, Tarrasch) treated doubled pawns as an objective defect to be avoided. The hypermoderns, Nimzowitsch above all, argued that dynamic factors routinely outweigh static structure. Modern engines side with neither absolutely, and will accept severe pawn defects for activity.

The practical form of the question is almost never 'should I allow doubled pawns' but 'which pawn should I recapture with', and the general answer — recapture towards the centre — has well-known exceptions: not when it tears open your own king's shelter, not when the other capture opens a file you can actually use, and not when it creates a chronic weakness on a file your opponent controls.
